1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Hedgehog System
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6.background: The ideas behind the Hedgehog set-up were originally developed in the English Opening, and it first became extensively analysed in the 1970s. Bobby Fischer adopted it with White against Ulf Andersson at Siegen in 1970, one of the first games to feature it, and his crushing win so impressed Andersson that he later became one of the foremost Hedgehog exponents himself.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and keeps every option open: it guards d4 and e5, so a challenge to the centre meets a ready defender. White has not yet decided between an early central advance and a slower build-up, and Black is free to choose its own set-up in return.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4.strategy: Grabs the centre at once and threatens to drive the f6-knight away with e5. White gives up the quiet flexibility of the knight development for space, betting that pawns on c4 and e4 plus the c3-knight hold the centre while Black, with no pawn in the middle yet, has to react accurately.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4.name: English Opening: Mikenas-Carls Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4.background: Also called the Flohr–Mikenas–Carls Variation, after Salo Flohr, Vladas Mikėnas and Carl Johan Margot Carls.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 d5.strategy: The principal answer: Black strikes at the centre immediately, and the pawn attacks both c4 and e4. The price is that the f6-knight stays exposed to an advance of White's e-pawn, so the game turns sharp at once and Black has to be accurate.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 Nc6.strategy: Pressures the centre with a piece instead of a pawn: the knight eyes d4 and e5, so an advance of the e-pawn simply loses it to a capture. Black commits a piece before the structure is clear and blocks the c-pawn, and White keeps the extra space.
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 Nc6.name: English Opening: Mikenas-Carls Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 Nc6.background: Known as the Kevitz Variation, after Alexander Kevitz.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 c5.strategy: Challenges the centre from the side: the pawn takes d4 away from White, so White cannot build a broad pawn centre without a fight, and Black heads for an unbalanced structure. The cost is time, since White gains space with tempo against the f6-knight before Black has developed much.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Stakes a claim to d4 with a pawn and heads for a symmetrical fight in which both sides contest d4 and d5. The play turns tactical, and Black keeps the freedom to choose the structure later.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which will press on the long diagonal towards e4 and the centre from a distance instead of occupying it with pawns. It is a solid set-up, at the price of a slower fight for the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4.strategy: Attacks the c3-knight, which guards both d5 and e4, and threatens to take it and double White's pawns. If Black takes, White gets the bishop pair in return for the damaged structure; Black gets quick development and a firm grip on the centre squares.
